Goethe. Johann Wolfgang von Goethe lived from 1749 to 1832. A German polymath—poet, novelist, dramatist, and natural philosopher—his work defined German Romanticism and influenced world literature for two centuries.

Born in Frankfurt, he spent most of his career in Weimar as court official and literary innovator.

At twenty-five, he published The Sorrows of Young Werther, an epistolary novel of a sensitive youth's unrequited love and despair. It became Europe's first literary sensation, spawning imitators and even suicides.

He spent sixty years developing Faust, publishing Part I in 1808 and completing Part II near his death in 1832. The work synthesizes classical and Romantic modes into a metaphysical drama about knowledge, power, and redemption.

In Faust, the scholar makes a pact with Mephistopheles for unlimited knowledge and pleasure. The drama explores whether such a bargain can be redeemed by human striving and love. The Faustian bargain became a cultural archetype.

He also wrote lyric poetry of the highest order. Poems like "Erlkönig," the Erlking, and "Über allen Gipfeln ist Ruh" became classics set to music by Schubert and Brahms.

Goethe worked as a minister and administrator in the court of the Duke of Saxe-Weimar, managing theater, education, and state business while writing. He pursued natural philosophy with scientific rigor, developing theories of color, plant morphology, and metamorphosis. Some of his ideas proved influential despite errors, such as rejecting Newtonian optics.

He bridged Enlightenment rationalism and Romantic emotion. His works celebrate human individuality, emotional depth, and creative genius while retaining humanistic moral seriousness.

By old age, he had become a cultural institution and the exemplar of German genius, profoundly influencing European thought and imagination.
